blocks.text: Great hummus is about texture as much as flavour. Four things do most of the work: a soft, warm base; blending in the right order; adding ice water slowly; and blending long enough to aerate.

items: Use the base warm where you can — warm chickpeas or freshly toasted sesame purée far smoother than cold.
Blend the base with tahini, lemon, garlic, salt and spices first, until completely smooth, before any water goes in.
With the motor running, stream in ice water a little at a time until the mix turns pale, glossy and holds soft ridges.
Keep blending for a full one to two minutes after the last water — that is what turns paste into a light, whipped cloud.

blocks.text: Rest the finished hummus for ten minutes before serving, and again check the salt and acidity — both mute as it sits.
The recipes use three families of base, and they behave differently.
Chickpea (the house base)
The classic. Creamy, nutty and neutral, built to carry bold flavours. Warm chickpeas and a full blend give the silkiest result.
Sesame
Sesame-seed hummus skips the beans entirely and leans on toasted and raw seeds blended to a loose butter. Intensely sesame-forward and very whippable.
Alternative bases

Beans, lentils, peas, edamame, avocado and roasted vegetables from beet to butternut. Roasted-vegetable bases need real browning and thorough draining, then a chill before serving for the cleanest flavour.
Tahini is the backbone of most hummus. Buy it runny and pourable, stir it well before measuring, and taste it — good tahini is nutty and only lightly bitter.

items: For sesame hummus, toast only half the seeds. The raw half keeps the flavour fresh and stops the batch turning bitter.
Let seeds run in the processor until they flow like loose butter before adding anything else; a dry paste never whips smooth.
A splash of ice water or a few ice cubes blended into tahini first lightens and pales it before the base goes in.

blocks.text: Add flavourings only once the base is completely smooth, then blend just long enough to combine so the addition stays vivid.

items: Wet ingredients — roasted peppers, caramelised onion, sun-dried tomato — must be well drained and fairly dry, or they thin the hummus and make it greasy.
Chilli pastes like harissa and chipotle build heat as the hummus rests; add a little at a time and taste.
When a recipe says "1 batch" of another recipe, make that recipe first (or hold back a little of its water so the base starts thicker), then fold the flavouring in.

blocks.text: Season salt last when adding cheese, olives, bacon or bagel seasoning — they already bring plenty.
Too thick
Blend in ice water a teaspoon at a time. It loosens quickly, so go slowly.
Too thin
Usually wet vegetables or water added too fast. Blend in a spoonful of tahini, or chill it — roasted-vegetable hummus firms up cold.
Bitter
Over-toasted sesame, too much raw garlic, or harsh tahini. Blend garlic with the lemon juice first so the acid tames it, and balance with a pinch more salt.
Grainy
Under-blended. Keep going, scraping the bowl, until there is no grittiness — then blend another minute for lightness.
Bland
Hummus needs more salt and acid than you expect. Add salt, then lemon, a little at a time, resting between.
Most hummus keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for about five days. Press plastic wrap onto the surface and add a thin film of olive oil to stop it drying.

items: Freeze plain hummus up to a month; thaw overnight and re-whip with a little ice water and oil.
Avocado hummus is best the day it is made and does not freeze.
Dairy, bacon or fresh-herb toppings are best added after thawing, not before freezing.
Serve at cool room temperature — straight from the fridge the flavour is muted.

blocks.text: Finish the bowl with a swirl of olive oil, a dusting of the recipe's main spice, and something with texture: warm chickpeas, toasted nuts, or chopped herbs.
The recipes are written by weight in grams for consistency, and yield roughly 500 g — about sixteen 30 g servings. Use the serving selector on a recipe to scale the quantities.
Nutrition figures are estimates calculated from the listed ingredients and are labelled as such. Always check ingredients against your own allergies and dietary needs.
A small amount of MSG appears in the house method as a savoury booster; it is optional and can be left out with a little extra salt.
